title: Authentication System
seoTitle: Design a User Login and Authentication System
description: Design website authentication — secure password storage, sessions vs. tokens, refresh tokens and revocation, MFA, and protecting login from abuse.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is an Authentication System?
blocks.text: Authentication proves who a user is. A login system lets people sign up, sign in with a password (and optionally a second factor), stay signed in across requests, and sign out — while keeping credentials safe.

items: Users should be able to sign up with email and password, and verify their email.
Users should be able to log in and stay logged in across requests and devices.
Users should be able to log out, including "log out of all devices".
Users should be able to reset a forgotten password and enable multi-factor authentication (MFA).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Security first: passwords stored so a database leak doesn't expose them; resistant to brute force and credential stuffing.
Authenticating each request must be fast (< 10ms) since every API call does it.
Highly available — if auth is down, the whole product is down.
Revocation (logout, password change) takes effect quickly.
**User**: email, password hash, MFA settings, status.
**Session / refresh token**: a long-lived credential tied to a device, revocable.
**Access token**: a short-lived token presented on every request.
**Verification / reset token**: one-time, expiring tokens sent by email.

blocks.text: The **Auth Service** hashes the password with a slow, salted algorithm — **Argon2id** or **bcrypt** — and stores only the hash. It then emails a one-time verification link containing a random token (stored hashed, with an expiry).
2) Log in and stay logged in
On login, verify the password hash (and MFA), then issue two credentials:

items: A short-lived **access token** (a signed JWT, ~15 minutes) the gateway can verify locally with a public key — no database lookup per request.
A long-lived **refresh token** (random, stored hashed in the Sessions table, sent as an HttpOnly, Secure cookie) used to obtain new access tokens.

blocks.text: Delete the session row (or all of a user's sessions). The refresh token stops working immediately; outstanding access tokens expire within minutes.
Reset emails contain a single-use, short-lived token; using it sets a new password and revokes all sessions. MFA uses TOTP (authenticator apps) or WebAuthn passkeys checked during login.

approach.text: Store passwords directly or encrypted with a key.

challenges.text: Any leak (or stolen key) exposes every password — and users reuse passwords elsewhere.
Salts stop rainbow tables, but fast hashes let attackers try billions of guesses per second on GPUs.

approach.text: Use Argon2id (or bcrypt) with a per-user salt and a work factor tuned to ~100ms per hash. Optionally add a **pepper** stored outside the database. Rehash on login when parameters are upgraded.

challenges.text: Login costs some CPU, so rate limiting matters even more.

approach.text: Store a session ID in a cookie and look it up in Redis on every request.

challenges.text: Instant revocation, but every request hits the session store — a hot dependency that must scale and stay up.

blocks.title: Short-lived JWT access tokens + revocable refresh tokens

approach.text: Gateways verify access tokens locally by signature (fast, no lookup). Revocation happens at refresh time, so its delay is bounded by the access-token lifetime. For urgent cases (compromised account), keep a small denylist of token IDs in a cache checked by the gateway. Rotate refresh tokens on each use and detect reuse to catch theft.

challenges.text: Up to ~15 minutes of access after logout unless the denylist is used.

blocks.text: 3) How do we protect login from abuse?

Rate limit by IP, account and device fingerprint; add exponential backoff and CAPTCHA after failures; check passwords against known-breached lists at signup; send new-device alerts; and return the same generic error for "no such user" and "wrong password" so attackers can't enumerate accounts.

quiz.question: Why use Argon2id or bcrypt instead of SHA-256 for passwords?
options: They are deliberately slow and memory-hard, making brute force expensive
quiz.explanation: Fast hashes allow billions of guesses per second on GPUs.

quiz.question: Why are access tokens short-lived?
options: They're verified without a lookup, so short lifetimes bound how long a revoked token works
quiz.explanation: Revocation is enforced at refresh time.

quiz.question: Where should a refresh token be stored in a browser?
quiz.explanation: HttpOnly cookies can't be read by injected scripts.

quiz.question: Why return the same error for unknown user and wrong password?
options: To prevent attackers enumerating which accounts exist
